name: openhmd
desc: Free and open source API and drivers for immersive technology
why: Drivers for VR headsets over USB HID; a real door into talking to immersive hardware, though the library itself is plumbing-adjacent.

brief.what_it_is: OpenHMD is a C library, with drivers, that lets applications read head tracking and related data from immersive hardware such as VR headsets (Oculus Rift, HTC Vive, PlayStation VR, Windows Mixed Reality, and others) and some VR controllers. It takes in raw USB/HID reports from those devices and presents them through one cross-platform C API that applications can enumerate, open and read from. The homepage says it also ships a Generic Android driver and an External Sensor driver, so you can feed in your own sensor data and still use its sensor fusion. Language bindings exist for Go, Java, .NET, Perl, Python and Rust.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the aim is to provide a Free and Open Source API and drivers for immersive technology, implementing support for as many devices as possible in a portable, cross-platform package. The blog credits years of reverse engineering, hacking and testing for each device's driver.
brief.how_it_works: Drivers talk to headsets and controllers over USB HID, using HIDAPI (hidraw on Linux). Each device has its own driver, and you choose which drivers to compile in at build time. Applications link the library and read tracking data through the public API, which is documented with Doxygen.

commands_seen.context: Configure the Meson build; the optional -Dexamples flag selects the example programs, and simple is the example listed as this brew package's executable.
Install the built library and files system-wide after the Meson build.
Change which drivers are compiled, using a comma-separated list such as rift, deepon, psvr, vive, nolo, wmr, xgvr, vrtek, external, android.
Create a build directory for the CMake build.
Enter the build directory before running cmake.
Configure the CMake build from the build directory; drivers are toggled with options such as OPENHMD_DRIVER_VRTEK.

brief.install_notes: You need HIDAPI, and either Meson with Ninja, GNU Autotools (only if building from the git repository), or CMake. On Linux, add a udev rule so you can open USB devices without root, then unplug and replug the device; the README points to a wiki list of udev rules. On Windows with CMake, a Visual Studio generator works; if you link statically with MinGW or MSVC, define OHMD_STATIC before including openhmd.h, but do not define it when using the DLL. By default all drivers except android are enabled. The homepage says v0.3 is the last release to support Autotools.
brief.standout: Instead of being one vendor's SDK, it is one open C API that reverse-engineered drivers for many competing headsets share, with a Boost license that lets it be linked into proprietary software. Its own project history is part of the appeal: the blog describes device support arriving through hackathons and reverse engineering.
brief.status: Unmaintained. The GitHub README opens with 'UNMAINTAINED' and says OpenHMD is 'currently NOT ACTIVELY MAINTAINED', asking people to open an issue if they want to maintain it. It also says driver development has largely moved to Monado. The latest release on the homepage is v0.3.0, dated 2019-07-12, and the homepage's newest blog post is from that date. I did not check commit history.
brief.caveats: The README says the project is not actively maintained, and development has largely moved to Monado. The 0.3.0 release notes say PSVR was disabled because of Windows and modern macOS issues, and that NOLO firmware versions were not all tested. Some peripherals (WMR controllers, PS Move, DualShock 4) work on Linux only through hidapi-hidraw. Oculus Rift CV1 positional tracking lives in a fork, not in this repository. The Unity plugin is labelled alpha, tested only on Unity 5.6 for Windows and Linux 64-bit, with no lens-correction shader. The homepage device table is not a full support list; the README sends you to a GitHub wiki for that. Several links on the homepage are to the old site and may be stale.
quotes: OpenHMD is currently NOT ACTIVELY MAINTAINED. If you are interested in maintaining OpenHMD, please open a github issue.
OpenHMD aims to provide a Free and Open Source API and drivers for immersive technology, such as head mounted displays with built in head tracking.
OpenHMD is released under the permissive Boost Software License (see LICENSE for more information), to make sure it can be linked and distributed with both free and non-free software.

judge.reason: Reverse-engineered USB/HID drivers make competing VR headsets readable through one API—a compelling peek into hardware protocols, despite the project’s unmaintained status.

entry.title: OpenHMD
entry.tldr: An open C library with reverse-engineered drivers that reads head tracking from many competing VR headsets through one API. Unmaintained, but a clear look at USB HID hardware.
entry.deeper_look:
OpenHMD is a C library that lets an application ask for head tracking and related data from VR headsets and some controllers. It covers devices such as the Oculus Rift, HTC Vive, PlayStation VR and Windows Mixed Reality. Raw USB HID reports come in from the hardware, and a single cross-platform API goes out: enumerate devices, open one, read from it.

The project exists because each vendor shipped its own SDK. The homepage states the aim as "a Free and Open Source API and drivers for immersive technology", supporting as many devices as possible in a portable package. Each device driver is the product of reverse engineering, hacking and testing, and the project's blog describes support arriving through hackathons. Drivers talk over HIDAPI (hidraw on Linux), and you pick which ones to compile in at build time.

The idea underneath is that a headset is mostly a stream of sensor packets. Once someone works out the report format, you can turn those bytes into orientation. There is also an External Sensor driver, so you can feed in your own sensor data and still use OpenHMD's sensor fusion. It is licensed under the Boost Software License so it can be linked into both free and proprietary software.

The project is old and marked unmaintained, with driver work having largely moved to Monado. The code is still a readable example of how a device family gets pulled out of vendor lock-in.
entry.install:
brew install openhmd
# Needs a supported VR headset or controller to show real data.
# On Linux, add a udev rule so USB devices open without root, then replug the device. The README links a wiki list of rules.

try_this.what_happens: Runs the bundled example executable's help, a starting point for reading from a connected device.
When building from source, selects which drivers to compile, using a comma-separated list such as rift, vive, psvr, wmr, external.

entry.whats_unique: It is one open C API shared by reverse-engineered drivers for many rival headsets, rather than one vendor's SDK. The permissive Boost license lets proprietary software link it.
entry.caveats: The README says it is not actively maintained, the last release (v0.3.0) is from July 2019, and you need compatible hardware to see anything.
